title: Body image and media messages
objectives: Explain why a post cannot show a person's full life or worth.
Spot a sales promise or a selected view in an invented message.
Choose a kind response and a safe route to adult help.
vocabulary: The thoughts and feelings a person has about their body. A person's worth does not depend on looks.
How a person values and respects themselves. It can change, and support can help.
Messages shared in print or on screens, such as adverts and posts.
Chosen from a larger set. A selected post leaves some things out.
A promise used to help sell something. A promise still needs evidence.

model.title: An invented advert
model.story: A plain text advert says: 'Buy this craft kit. Look perfect. Feel sure every day.' A note says: 'This advert sells a craft kit. It gives no evidence for its promise.' An invented learner sees the advert and begins to feel less sure about joining a club.
model.reasoning: The message links buying a kit and looking a certain way with feeling sure. It gives no proof. A kit cannot promise how someone will feel each day. The learner's worth does not depend on looks or buying it. A fair rewrite is: 'This kit has craft materials. People can enjoy making things in different ways.' The learner could pause the advert and talk to a trusted adult.

cases.title: A promise in a made up advert
cases.story: An invented advert says: 'Buy this photo light. Everyone will like you.' The small print says: 'The light has two brightness settings.' The advert gives no evidence that buying it changes friendships.
questions: Which line describes the item, and which line makes a promise about being liked?
What evidence is missing from the friendship promise?
Write a fair line that describes the item without judging a person's looks or worth.
cases.answer: Two brightness settings describes the item within this invented card. 'Everyone will like you' is a sales promise, with no evidence that a light can make everyone like a person. Accept: 'This light has two settings for taking a photo.' It must not link buying the light to worth, popularity or a required look. The learner can leave the advert and ask a trusted adult if the message causes worry.

cases.title: A selected post
cases.story: A made up post says: 'Ready first time. Every day is easy.' A source note for this classroom story says: 'The creator chose one picture from many tries. They left out the practice and the times they asked for help.' No real picture or account is used.
questions: What does the source note show was left out?
Why can this one post not show the creator's full day or feelings?
Rewrite the caption so it allows practice, help and different experiences.
cases.answer: The post leaves out other tries, practice and help. One chosen picture and caption cannot show every part of a day or prove that a person always feels sure. The supplied source note supports this answer in this story; do not assume every real post is edited or false. Accept: 'One chosen moment after practice. Asking for help is fine.' No pupil should compare their appearance or life with the invented creator.

cases.title: A kind response to a hurtful reply
cases.story: A learner shares a made up notice about a drama club. One invented reply judges who should join by their looks. Another reply says: 'People can join, learn and ask for help in different ways.' The learner stops reading the hurtful replies and asks a trusted adult what to do.
questions: Which reply respects people without judging bodies?
What can the learner do without arguing with or passing on the hurtful reply?
Who could help if the first adult is not available?
cases.answer: The inclusive reply respects people without judging looks. The learner can stop engaging, move away from the item and tell a trusted adult. Adult help can support a suitable mute, block or report step if needed. They do not have to reply, prove their worth, confront anyone or copy and spread the hurtful item. If the first adult is unavailable or does not help, another trusted adult or the safeguarding lead can help.

hinge.question: An invented advert says buying an item will make everyone like a learner. What is the safest conclusion?
options: A. The learner must buy it to be worth liking.
B. The advert makes a promise without proof. The learner's worth does not depend on buying it.
C. Every advert and every post must be false.
hinge.reason: The card gives no evidence for the promise about being liked. It does not define anyone's worth. It also does not prove that every advert is false.
hinge.parallel_question: A post shows one selected moment. Does it prove that the person's whole life is easy?
parallel_options: A. No. One chosen moment cannot show a whole life or all feelings.
B. Yes. A clear post shows every part of the person's life.
hinge.parallel_reason: A selected moment leaves other events and feelings unseen. The learner can pause rather than compare bodies or lives.

Supported: Use the model and word bank. For case 1, point to the item fact or the sales promise. Choose: 'The light has two settings' or 'Everyone will like you'. Explain one choice with: 'This promise has no proof that ___.'.
For case 2, choose what was left out: practice and help, or nothing. Use the frame: 'One post cannot show ___.'. Keep the source note and model visible. Do not judge anyone's body.

For case 3, choose the kind reply and one safe step: stop engaging and tell a trusted adult. Point, say, draw or type a plan for the invented learner. Name the safeguarding lead or another trusted adult if the first adult is not available.
Independent: Use the three invented cards. For case 1, separate an item fact from a sales promise. Explain the missing evidence. Write a fair advert line that gives item facts without linking looks or buying to worth.
For case 2, explain how the source note changes the message. Write a caption that allows practice and help. State one limit of what a post can show.
For case 3, choose a kind response and a safe help plan. Explain why the learner need not reply or forward the hurtful item. Give a second adult route if the first adult is unavailable.
Aspire: Compare the model advert with case 1. Explain how each tries to link an item with feelings or approval. Separate what the card supports from what remains unproved. Rewrite one claim without body judgement.
Use case 2 to explain the effect of selection. State why the source note supports this case without proving that all posts are false. Write a fair caption and explain how it reduces pressure.

For case 3, explain a safe response if hurtful replies continue or the first adult does not help. Keep the focus on adult support, the learner's right to respect and not spreading the item. No confrontation or personal detail is needed.

evidence_rows: Distinguishes an item fact from an unsupported promise, using an invented card.
Explains a limit of one post and offers a body neutral line that allows practice or help.
Chooses a kind response, disengagement and a trusted adult or safeguarding lead route; adds an alternative adult if needed.
misconceptions: A polished post proves that a person is always happy or confident.
A selected post cannot show a full life or every feeling. Use the supplied source note for this case; do not guess about real people.
A person must change their looks or buy an item to deserve respect.
Everyone deserves respect. Looks, approval and purchases do not decide a person's worth. A kind response avoids judging bodies.
teaching_points: Body image concerns thoughts and feelings about the body. People deserve respect whatever they look like. The class does not rate or compare bodies.
An advert may try to sell an item by promising feelings or approval. Separate the item description from a promise and ask what evidence supports it.
A post may show a selected view. In the supplied story, the source note shows omitted practice and help. One post cannot show a whole life; this does not make every post false.

A body neutral rewrite describes the item or activity without judging looks. If a message causes worry or hurt, the invented learner can stop engaging and ask a trusted adult or the safeguarding lead for help.
